section_summary: This section centers on the attempted clandestine shipment of Mexican mercury to Japan aboard the Azuma Maru, including consular reports, Mexican press coverage, diplomatic protests, and evidence identifying the suspected participants. It also documents Japanese efforts to obtain strategic materials from Latin America and the Netherlands East Indies amid freezing orders and financial restrictions. A substantial group of policy memoranda compares American, British, and Dutch controls on petroleum, cotton, iron ore, manganese, and other exports to Japan and urges coordinated economic action.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the Embassy in Mexico concerning the Azuma Maru mercury case
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to express grave concern to Mexico over the attempted shipment of mercury to Japan and to seek stronger preventive controls.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that the accumulation of mercury at Manzanillo, despite Mexico's July 10 export decree, strongly suggested an intended clandestine shipment to Japan. It praises the Vice Consul's vigilance, suggests direct government control of mercury stocks, and leaves the precise presentation to the Embassy and Ransom's discretion.

subfiles.title: Commendation of Vice Consul Henry A. Hoyt
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Commends Hoyt for preventing the attempted smuggling of mercury to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State commends Vice Consul Henry Hoyt's October 5 and 7 telegrams, whose prompt action apparently stopped the concealed mercury smuggling attempt.

subfiles.title: Trade between Japan, Chile, and Brazil
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on Japan's curtailed trade with Chile and Brazil following the American freezing order.
subfiles.summary: Chilean and Brazilian representatives reported no Japanese threats or reprisals, but trade had fallen sharply because of depleted credits, limited Japanese exports, financial controls, and shipping difficulties. The telegram reviews nitrate, copper, cotton, and silk transactions, possible barter arrangements, and Japan's unsuccessful effort to secure Panama Canal passage for Brazilian vessels.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo telegram 1562
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the Embassy's report on Japanese commerce with Chile and Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Tokyo telegram 1562: Japan's trade with Chile is limited by exhausted credits and weak demand, nitrate and copper purchases are cut, and Brazil trade is possible in cotton but hampered by the long route and Panama Canal closure.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Tokyo trade telegram to the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards the paraphrase of Tokyo telegram 1562 concerning Japan's trade with Chile and Brazil.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury the October 4 Tokyo telegram on commercial relations between Japan, Chile and Brazil.

subfiles.title: Mexico City agents in the Manzanillo mercury transaction
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Consulate, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Identifies Ramón Obregón and Luis Basuto as Mexico City agents connected with the mercury shipment.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt: mercury flask count undetermined; he names two Mexico City agents, notes Llorens expects another bronze shipment, and says the Consulate General was informed.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Hoyt's October 7 noon telegram
subfiles.about: Restates the identification of the Mexico City agents and the possibility of another disguised shipment.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Hoyt's October 7 telegram: flask total undetermined, agents Luis Basuto and Ramon Obregon, Llorens expects another shipment, Consulate General notified.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Manzanillo mercury telegrams to Export Control
subfiles.from: Edward L. Reed, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards three telegram paraphrases about mercury concealed in drums labeled as bronze.
subfiles.summary: Reed sends Export Control Hoyt's October 5 and 7 telegrams on an attempt to export mercury from Manzanillo in drums labeled bronze.

subfiles.title: Identification of A. Z. Phillips
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Consulate, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Reports reliable information that A. Z. Phillips was the person behind the mercury transaction.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt states emphatically that A. Z. Phillips of Mexico City was involved in the shipment; the Embassy and Consulate General were advised.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting supplemental raw-cotton statistics
subfiles.about: Sends a statistical supplement emphasizing Brazilian and Peruvian cotton trade.
subfiles.summary: Dent sends a supplement to his earlier raw-cotton memorandum on Japan, India and the U.S., focused on Brazil and Peru.

subfiles.title: Raw Cotton Statistics—Supplemental
subfiles.about: Compiles Japanese cotton imports and Brazilian and Peruvian cotton exports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum breaks down Japanese cotton imports by origin and provides multiyear export figures for Brazil and Peru. It also lists monthly Brazilian and Peruvian shipments to Japan during 1941 and notes additional cotton sent to Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of cotton statistics
subfiles.about: Thanks Dent for the supplemental cotton memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein acknowledges Dent's October 1 letter and its enclosed cotton statistics. He states that the figures were very useful.

subfiles.title: Shipments of mercury from Spain to Japan via Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, American Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports Spanish mercury shipments routed through Argentina and the arrangements used to pay for them.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy learned that two lots of 5,000 mercury flasks each had reached Buenos Aires from Spain, with the first already shipped onward to Japan. Payment for the first consignment used blocked Argentine pesos acquired through transfers of Japanese dollar balances, with the Banco de la Provincia guaranteeing the transaction.

subfiles.title: Standard Vacuum remittances and Netherlands East Indies oil
subfiles.about: Reports a Foreign Funds Control conversation about Japanese remittances and financing an oil shipment from the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Singer asks about a $557,000 Japanese remittance and a $105,000 oil deal, saying the remittance predated Standard's demand for old debts; Indies authorities would license export if the U.S. approves financing.

subfiles.title: Suspension of New Caledonian nickel-ore shipments
subfiles.to: G. T. Bridgman, Metals Reserve Company
subfiles.about: Forwards information that nickel-ore shipments from New Caledonia to Japan had been suspended.
subfiles.summary: Finletter encloses A. D. Marris's September 27 letter apparently confirming suspension of New Caledonian nickel-ore exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Mexican investigation of the attempted mercury export
subfiles.about: Reports Mexico's promise of a thorough investigation into the attempted illicit export of mercury.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy presented the Department's concerns to the Mexican Foreign Minister, who said that he and the President shared them. The President directed the Treasury and Attorney General to investigate fully, with the Foreign Minister overseeing the inquiry regardless of the rank or influence of those responsible.

subfiles.title: War Department cable on the Manzanillo seizure
subfiles.to: War Department; copy to Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports publicity surrounding the seizure of mercury concealed aboard a Japanese vessel at Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: War Department cable: 347 drums manifested as bronze parts each held five mercury flasks; the consul witnessed opening, and Mexico embargoed the shipment.

subfiles.title: British inquiry into strategic-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Finletter's request for information on strategic-material shipments to Japan, especially from Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Marris thanks Finletter for his September 22 letter; the British Embassy is seeking more information.

subfiles.title: Attempted shipment of mercury at Manzanillo on the Azuma Maru
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Gives a detailed account of the discovery of mercury concealed in drums manifested as bronze and encloses press reports and a photograph.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt describes noticing the unusual weight and handling of the drums, alerting customs with the British Vice Consul, and discovering five mercury flasks in the first opened drum. He identifies Llorens as the local shipper and A. Z. Phillips as the suspected principal, possibly working with Nagabuchi, and suggests that a September shipment on the Heiyo Maru may also have contained mercury. Four Spanish-language newspaper clippings describe the case, official investigations, and suspected earlier smuggling, while the final enclosure identifies a photograph of the 347 drums.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese funds for petroleum purchases
subfiles.to: Division of American Republics / Dean Acheson
subfiles.about: References a conversation about transferring Japanese South American funds to buy oil for two tankers in San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Norman Towson's interview with Nishiyama on free funds for oil, as Nishiyama tried moving funds from South America to the U.S.; filed under frozen credits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Netherlands East Indies petroleum shipment
subfiles.about: References a conversation with Baron van Boetzelaer about petroleum shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a memorandum of Baron van Boetzelaer's conversation with Dean Acheson on a Netherlands East Indies petroleum shipment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese inquiry about American petroleum exports
subfiles.about: References a conversation with the Japanese Embassy counselor about paying for nonprohibited petroleum exports.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a counselor asked whether Japanese firms could export permitted petroleum if Japanese dollar balances in Latin America moved to the U.S.; filed under frozen credits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: proposed Chilean cement-for-minerals barter
subfiles.about: References information on Japanese efforts to arrange a barter of cement for Chilean minerals.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a British Embassy note on a proposed Japan-Chile cement-for-minerals barter, filed in the defense file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: report of shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: References a report listing shipments to Japan on specified dates.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a report of shipments to Japan was submitted; original filed elsewhere in the Japan equipment records.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: German financing for Argentine hides
subfiles.about: References information on Japan's attempt to borrow German funds to pay for hides purchased in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japanese efforts to get German funds for partial payment on Argentine hides, from a British Embassy note.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Mauricio Hochschild's mineral-industry activities
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Chile, Claude G. Bowers
subfiles.about: References a despatch transmitting a British Embassy letter on Mauricio Hochschild's mineral activities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: report on Mauricio Hochschild's mineral-industry activities, despatch 1894 and the personal-name file.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs recommendation on pre-freezing cotton
subfiles.about: Supports exchanging Japanese-owned cotton bought before the freezing order for the release of American-owned goods in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs concurs in releasing pre-freezing Japanese cotton if Japan releases American property reciprocally, noting India and Britain allowed pre-freezing credits and obligations.

subfiles.title: Political Relations comments on petroleum, iron ore, and cotton policy
subfiles.about: Comments on proposed export policies and recommends guarded communications with Britain and the Netherlands.
subfiles.summary: Political Relations concurs on petroleum and iron ore but advises describing American intentions only in broad guarded terms and postponing cotton action, telling the British.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on continuing the suspension of exports
subfiles.about: Recommends maintaining the effective stoppage of petroleum and cotton exports and quietly controlling Philippine iron-ore licenses.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs favors continuing no petroleum or cotton exports to Japan without declaring a total ban, and referring all Philippine iron-ore applications to Washington while withholding action.

subfiles.title: Trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reviews Allied restrictions on trade with Japan and recommends coordinated action on petroleum, iron ore, and cotton.
subfiles.summary: Acheson concludes that British, Dutch, and American trade with Japan was virtually at a standstill, although American policy remained less clearly articulated. He recommends rejecting Japanese payment proposals, jointly ending petroleum exports, coordinating a prohibition on Malayan and Philippine iron ore, and matching British cotton restrictions. He warns that indecision could destroy the newly achieved common front against Japan.

subfiles.title: Restrictions on Japanese trade and payments in the British Empire
subfiles.to: Secretary of State / Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Compares British Empire and United States restrictions on Japanese assets, trade, payments, and shipping.
subfiles.summary: The survey compares blocked-account rules, export and import controls, trade with occupied China, and bunkering practices. It details remaining exceptions for Malayan ore, Indian cotton, and selected American products, then reviews conditions in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Burma, and Eire. Overall trade with Japan was nearly immobilized throughout the Empire.

subfiles.title: Restrictions on Japanese trade and payments in the Netherlands East Indies
subfiles.from: Adviser on Political Relations, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reviews Dutch East Indies proposals for restricting strategic exports and petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that trade had effectively stopped and lists commodities the Governor General believed should be embargoed or severely restricted. It reports Dutch willingness to end petroleum exports if the United States acted similarly and describes conditions demanding Japanese withdrawal from southern Indochina. The author concludes that the Indies would probably pattern its policy closely on a definitive American program.

subfiles.title: British Embassy memorandum on a common imperial policy toward Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that a common British Empire policy had reduced trade with Japan almost to a standstill.
subfiles.summary: India was allowing only limited cotton exports against pre-freezing credits, while some Malayan iron ore and manganese continued pending coordinated Philippine action. The Netherlands East Indies had stopped oil shipments and allowed only small quantities of previously paid goods, with Britain and the Netherlands aiming at near-complete immobilization of trade.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to Tokyo transmitting the British policy memorandum
subfiles.about: Drafts the transmission of the British Embassy memorandum on the Empire-wide trade policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the September 22 British Embassy memorandum for the Ambassador's strictly confidential information. The attached copy describes the near-cessation of British and Dutch trade with Japan and the limited exceptions still in force.

subfiles.title: Final instruction to the American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends the British Embassy's September 22 memorandum on the common British Empire policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Secretary forwards the memorandum to Tokyo for strictly confidential information, also distributed to Chongqing, Beijing, Canberra and Bangkok.
